passage: Siddiq had heard it at least six times that week in the office kitchen in Cape Town: the number 12 bus route was being scrapped at the end of the month. Thabo had said it. The receptionist had said it. Someone had pinned a sad note about it on the board. Siddiq was halfway through an email to his team suggesting they move their meeting times when he stopped, fingers above the keys. Have I actually checked this, he wondered, or have I just heard it a lot? He opened the transport department's own notices page. The route wasn't being scrapped. It was being moved two streets over for three weeks of road repairs. He deleted the email and walked to the kitchen. "Thabo, the 12 isn't going anywhere. Just a detour." Thabo frowned. "But everyone said..." "I know. I believed it too, because everyone said it."

qa.q: What was really happening to the number 12 route?
qa.a: It was being moved two streets over for three weeks of road repairs.

qa.q: What made Siddiq stop in the middle of the email?
qa.a: Siddiq wondered whether the claim had actually been checked or only heard many times, and that doubt was enough to pause.

qa.q: Which step turned the rumour into something Siddiq could rely on?
qa.a: Opening the transport department's own notices page, one first-hand source, instead of counting how many people had said it.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel when Siddiq brings the news?
qa.a: Thabo is surprised and a little defensive, but Siddiq admitting to believing it too makes it easier for Thabo to accept.

grounding: A young man asks whether he has checked a rumour or only heard it often, reads the official notice, and admits he had believed it too.

passage: Preeti was making slides in the school staffroom for Saturday's parent workshop when she typed it: "Every child has a learning style: visual, listening or hands-on. Teach to it!" She had heard that line at every training since college, on posters, and from Vijay across the table only yesterday. She looked at it, then typed a small note in the margin: Checked, or just heard a lot? Honestly, just heard. At lunch she read one long review by education researchers, the original, not a summary. It said matching lessons to a child's preferred style hadn't shown the gains people claimed, and that mixing ways of teaching helped everyone. She deleted the slide. "Vijay," she said, "you know the learning styles thing? I've repeated it for years. Turns out familiar isn't the same as true." Vijay put his tea down. "Show me."

qa.q: What note did Preeti type in the margin?
qa.a: Checked, or just heard a lot?

qa.q: What was Preeti realising when she answered her own note with "Honestly, just heard"?
qa.a: She was realising, a little uncomfortably, that the line felt true only because she had met it at every training, on posters and from Vijay, not because she had ever checked it.

qa.q: Why was reading the original review a better choice than asking around the staffroom?
qa.a: Asking around would only bring back the same repeated claim, while one first-hand source showed what had actually been found.

qa.q: How might the parents at Saturday's workshop be affected by Preeti's choice?
qa.a: They will hear a better-grounded message and won't go home trying to sort their children into styles the research did not support.

grounding: A teacher questions a familiar claim before a workshop, reads one original review, and admits familiarity had stood in for checking.

passage:
Dear Zubin,
You forwarded the "free metro on Sundays from next month" message to the family group this morning, and I nearly replied "Finally!" I'd heard it from Masi, from two colleagues and from our building guard. It felt settled.
Then I asked myself something I'm trying to make a habit: have I checked this, or have I just heard it a lot? Just heard it, honestly. So I went to the metro corporation's own website and read their notices. Nothing about free Sundays. There's a discount for students, that's all.
I'm not writing to scold you. I nearly shared it myself, and the only reason it felt true was that it was everywhere. Could you post a short correction in the group? Masi listens to you more than to me.
Love,
Ritu

qa.a: Nothing about free Sundays, only a discount for students.

qa.q: Why did the free-metro claim feel settled to Ritu at first?
qa.a: Ritu had heard it from Masi, two colleagues and the building guard, so it felt true simply because it was everywhere.

qa.q: What does Ritu ask Zubin to do, and why is that a good next step?
qa.a: Post a short correction in the family group, since Masi listens to Zubin more, which can stop the rumour spreading.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel reading the email?
qa.a: Zubin might feel a little embarrassed, but Ritu admitting to nearly sharing it too makes the correction feel friendly rather than like a scolding. 🙂

grounding: A young adult asks whether a claim was checked or just heard often, reads the official source, and admits it only felt true from repetition.

passage: So, Lalit, you asked why I didn't sign the petition. Here's Chaitanya's slightly embarrassing answer. For a month I'd heard that the old municipal library near our college was being knocked down for a mall. Heard it from the chai stall, from two colleagues, from my mother's building group. I believed it completely. I even started a sad post about it. Then I stopped and asked myself: have I actually checked this, or have I just heard it a lot? Just heard it. Every single time. So I went to the corporation's website and found the ward's works notice. It wasn't demolition. It was repairs to the roof, three months, then it reopens. I sat there feeling a bit foolish. The claim felt true because it was familiar, and familiar told me nothing. I deleted my post and sent the notice to the chai stall uncle.

qa.a: It said the library was getting roof repairs for three months and would then reopen.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya feel a bit foolish after reading the notice?

qa.q: What habit helped Chaitanya most here, and why?
qa.a: Asking "have I checked this, or just heard it a lot?" and then going to the primary source, the ward's works notice, instead of relying on repetition.

qa.q: How might the chai stall uncle react to getting the notice?

passage: I'm Gopika, and I sit opposite Sangeeta at the design agency. For two weeks everyone on our floor had been saying the office would switch to a four-day week from April. You heard it at the coffee machine, in the lift, in the lunch queue. Last Tuesday, someone asked Sangeeta about it and she started to nod, then stopped. She said, "Actually, I've heard that maybe twenty times, but I've never read it anywhere." Then she opened the staff portal and searched for the HR circular. She read it out to our row: the four-day week was a pilot, for one small team, for one month. She laughed and said, "I'd have sworn it was for all of us. Hearing it a lot doesn't make it so." I don't know if she was annoyed, but she sent the link to our group straight away.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta's stopping mid-nod suggest she realised?

"Huh," said Sumit. "Everyone said six months."

passage:
Zeenat, you asked how I got so fussy about facts. Sit, I'll tell you.
I was twenty-five, a junior at a small city paper, writing a Sunday piece on the old clock tower. Everybody in the city knew it was built by the British in 1890. My editor said it. The tour guides said it. It was even painted on a sign near the market.
I had the line typed. Then, late at night, something nagged me. I asked myself, "Have I actually seen this anywhere official, or have I just heard it a hundred times?"
Next morning I went to the municipal records room. Dusty ledgers, one fan. The tower was paid for by three local cloth merchants, and finished in 1921.
I went to my editor feeling foolish, admitting I'd nearly printed a thing only because it sounded familiar. He printed the ledger photo.
I'm Raghav, and that sign is still wrong, by the way.

qa.q: Where did Raghav go to check the clock tower's history?
qa.a: To the municipal records room.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when something nagged him late at night?
qa.a: Raghav felt uneasy and doubtful, sensing that hearing the claim a hundred times was not the same as having checked it.

qa.q: What choice was the turning point in Raghav's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Going to the municipal records room was the turning point, because one primary source showed the familiar story was wrong before it was printed.

qa.q: How might the editor have seen the young Raghav after the ledger?
qa.a: The editor seems to have respected Raghav's care, since he printed the ledger photo instead of the familiar version.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young adult, the speaker asked if a familiar claim had been checked and went to a primary source.

passage:
The client call started in twelve minutes, and Francis still had one slide to finish. The line he had typed was one he'd heard in every marketing workshop: "Most customers only read the first line of an email."
Shalini leaned over his desk. "Nice. Punchy."
Francis stared at it. He'd heard it from trainers, from his old boss, from videos. He couldn't remember reading it anywhere real. "Have I checked this, or just heard it a lot?" he muttered.
With nine minutes left, he opened the company's own email report from last quarter. Most people had opened, scrolled and clicked links far down the page.
He deleted the line and typed the real figure from their own report instead.
"You've lost your punchy line," Shalini said.
"It was only punchy because it was familiar," Francis said, a bit sheepish. "It wasn't checked."

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the call when the passage begins?
qa.a: Twelve minutes.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when he admitted the line was only familiar?
qa.a: He felt a bit sheepish, but settled that he had caught the mistake before the client saw it.

qa.q: What would you advise someone preparing slides under time pressure, based on Francis?
qa.a: Pause on any line that feels obviously true, ask if it has been checked, and use one real source even if it is less catchy.

qa.q: How does Shalini see the change to the slide?
qa.a: She seems a little disappointed to lose a catchy line, though Francis's reason may make her think twice about such lines too.

grounding: It shows an adult under time pressure questioning a familiar claim, checking the team's own data and admitting familiarity is not truth.

On Sunday night in her Mumbai flat, Jyoti was preparing Monday's science lesson on winter clothing. She typed: "We lose most of our body heat through our heads, so always wear a cap." Then she paused. Had she ever checked that, or just heard it every winter from her mother, her aunties, the school nurse?
She pulled out her college physiology textbook and read the section twice. Heat loss depended on how much skin was uncovered, the book said; the head wasn't special. She deleted the line.
On Monday she told her colleague Nikita, "I was about to teach something I'd only heard a lot." Nikita laughed. "I've said that cap line to my own kids." "Me too," Jyoti said. "Familiar isn't the same as true."

qa.q: What did Jyoti check the claim in?
qa.a: Her college physiology textbook.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she paused over the line?
qa.a: She felt doubtful and curious, unsure whether she had ever checked the claim or only heard it often.

qa.q: Which question helped Jyoti most?
qa.a: Whether she had checked the claim or just heard it a lot, which sent her to a primary source before teaching.

qa.a: Nikita seems amused and a bit sheepish, realising she had repeated the same line.

I'm Rajni, and I host a weekly quiz night with Divyansh. Last month I wrote a question: "True or false: the Great Wall of China can be seen from space with the naked eye." Answer: true. I'd heard it since school, in textbooks, on quiz shows, from my uncle.
Then I stopped. Had I ever actually verified it, or just heard it a thousand times? I went to an original source: interviews with astronauts on the space agency's own site. Most said they couldn't see it at all. I changed the answer to false.
When Divyansh read it out on the night, half the room groaned in disbelief. I told them, "Me too. It felt true because I'd heard it so often." It became our most-discussed question ever.

passage:
Monday night

Nearly said something silly at the society meeting today. Nitin was arguing that we should stop the kids playing in the rain because 'getting wet gives you a fever'. I opened my mouth to agree. It's what my Amma always said, and her Amma. Then I stopped. Have I actually checked this, or just heard it a lot? Just heard it, a thousand times. So I said, 'I'm not sure that's true. Can we check before we make a rule?' At home I looked at the children's hospital's own advice page. It says fevers are caused by infections, not by rain itself. That's all. I sent the link to the group. Nitin replied, 'Huh. My whole family believes that.' So did mine. Believing it for years doesn't make it checked.

Lakshmi

qa.q: Whose advice page did Lakshmi check?
qa.a: The children's hospital's own advice page.

qa.q: What made Lakshmi stop before agreeing with Nitin?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt a flicker of doubt, noticing the claim was familiar from Amma rather than something checked.

qa.a: Asking 'can we check before we make a rule?' keeps a familiar belief from becoming a rule without evidence.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel after reading the link?
qa.a: Nitin may feel surprised and a bit unsettled, since his whole family has believed it for years.

By Tuesday Manjula had heard it three times: at the tea stall by the bus stand, from the tailor, and from her own aunt. The college scholarship form closes this Friday. Ankita, from the house opposite, was already panicking over missing documents.
Manjula stopped her cycle at the canal bridge. Did she actually know this, or had she only heard it a lot? She could not name a single person who had read the notice.
So she rode the four kilometres to the block office and found the printed circular on the board. Last date: the 30th, not Friday.
Back home she told Ankita, a little sheepishly, "I'd have sworn it was Friday. Everyone said so. Hearing it everywhere didn't make it right."
Ankita laughed and put the kettle back on.
